extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / experimental physicists or opticians attempting to reproduce Newton's prism experiment
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, stepwise instructions and success criteria for reproducing Newton's prism (sunlight dispersion) experiment and the expected observations when set up correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Get a prism with an angle about 60 or 65 degrees (Newton used ≈63°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the angle is about 63 degrees results match Newton's description. If larger or smaller (e.g., 30, 40, 50, or 70°) the refraction changes accordingly and the image will be longer or shorter. If the prism is nearly equilateral (as commonly sold) use the largest angle but ensure refraction is made by the two planes that comprehend that angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism axis perpendicular to incoming rays
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the prism so that its axis is perpendicular to the incident rays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A little error in this point makes no sensible variation of the effect, but perpendicularity is the intended orientation (see reference to N° 84).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal refractions on both sides of the prism
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the prism so that the refractions on both sides are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is done by turning the prism about its axis and 'staying it when you see the image rest between two contrary motions' (i.e., rotate until image motion in opposite directions balances). Small errors here are tolerable and 'can do no hurt.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism placement relative to aperture (close to the hole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the prism close to the hole (contiguous to the shutter/hole was Newton's arrangement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton usually placed the prism close behind the hole; he states the prism and hole were contiguous and represents it so in the figures. However, the hole may be at some distance from the prism provided the light is arranged so the beam appears round on exiting the prism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aperture (hole) size
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an aperture roughly 1/4 of an inch in diameter (Newton's hole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton used a hole of 1/4 inch but says 'there needs no curiosity' — the hole may be of any other size provided the arrangement ensures the light appears of a round form when intercepted perpendicularly on exit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light source and weather conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct sunlight (clear days preferred); slight cloudiness tolerable if the sun shines distinctly through the cloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton emphasizes the experiment was 'tried in the sun's light' and compares breadth of image to the sun's diameter. He notes that using a lens on the prism made straight edges more distinct — a circumstance incompatible with a bright cloud source — supporting that the sun (not diffuse cloud) is the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection distance and perpendicular incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Project the refracted light perpendicular onto a wall or paper at ~20 feet or more from the prism (Newton used ~22 feet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At about 20–22 feet, when the refracted light falls perpendicularly on the screen, the characteristic oblong image appears. The perpendicular incidence and sufficient distance are part of reproducing Newton's 'experimentum crucis.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected image characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When set up correctly, the refracted light appears oblong cross to the axis of the prism, red at one end and violet at the other, length about five times the breadth (varies with refraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other expected features: sides straight and parallel, ends confused but seeming semicircular. The length-to-breadth ratio depends on the prism's refraction; transverse (not parallel) image orientation is required for red and blue to fall at opposite ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure refraction occurs through the intended prism faces/planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the prism so refraction is produced by the two planes that include the chosen angle of the prism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using an equilateral prism, be sure the two planes that 'comprehend this angle' are the ones effecting the refraction; an incorrect choice of faces can produce erroneous expectations about image length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of additional optics to sharpen features
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a lens to the prism can make the straight edges of the oblong image more distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton reports that applying a lens to the prism produced clearer straight edges than without the lens; he uses this as evidence that the experiment requires directed sunlight rather than diffused light from a cloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for small setup errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Small inaccuracies (in axis perpendicularity, exact equality of refractions, hole size, slight cloudiness) do not materially spoil the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton repeatedly notes that 'a little error' in axis or equality of refractions 'makes no sensible variation' and that hole size or slight cloudiness (provided the sun shines through) 'cannot much prejudice the experiment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrations and manipulations to test transverse image nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform further manipulations (e.g., use two cross prisms or a second prism of contrary refraction) to verify the image is transverse and to transform the oblong into a round image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton describes experiments (N° 83, N° 88) where a second prism with opposite refraction turns the long image into a round one — an operation impossible if the image were parallel as some critics supposed. This is both a diagnostic and a demonstration of different refrangibility.
